ContraSolver: Self-Alignment of Language Models by Resolving Internal Preference Contradictions

Xu Zhang*, Xunjian Yin *, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗Code ↗

A model's preferences can contradict each other; ContraSolver finds cycles in those judgments and selects reliable comparisons to improve alignment through DPO.

01 / The research question

A collection of plausible judgments can be inconsistent

Preference training commonly treats responses as if each had a single underlying quality score. That implies a coherent ordering for a fixed prompt. Yet a model judging pairs separately can prefer A to B, B to C, and C to A. Each local decision may look plausible, while the collection supplies conflicting supervision.

Confidence-only selection does not ask where a comparison sits in this structure. It may retain redundant preferences and miss comparisons that explain a contradiction elsewhere. ContraSolver instead makes the response set a directed graph. An arrow records a preference; a directed cycle exposes a conflict that cannot be represented by one consistent ranking.

02 / Explore the idea

Algorithm 1 · illustrative judgments

Which of the model’s own judgments become training pairs?

Five responses to one prompt and ten pairwise judgments. Flip a judgment or change its illustrative confidence: the paper’s graph algorithm reruns and reports the spanning tree, the contradictions, the resulting order, and the pairs it would use for DPO.

One prompt, five sampled continuations · illustrative

  1. A…premise, but the cast turns it into a warm, genuinely funny film.

The prefix comes from the paper’s case study (Appendix, Table 8); the continuations are written for this demo. The model judges each pair by asking which continuation is more positive (Table 5), averaging over both answer orders. Its confidence is the edge weight. In this example two judgments, D ≻ B and E ≻ C, disagree with the evident order of the texts.

Click a judgment or an arrow to flip it; − and + change its confidence by 0.05. Try flipping both disagreeing judgments, or raising E ≻ C above D ≻ E.

What the algorithm did

  1. Tree Kruskal keeps the strongest connected comparisons: A ≻ E 0.95, B ≻ E 0.92, B ≻ C 0.90, C ≻ D 0.88.
  2. Pass 1 Reverse loop: D ≻ B 0.59 contradicts the kept chain B ≻ C ≻ D and is marked contradictory; heuristic: B ≻ C, C ≻ D. Forward loop: adds D ≻ E 0.86.
  3. Pass 2 Reverse loop: E ≻ C 0.64 contradicts the kept chain C ≻ D ≻ E and is marked contradictory; heuristic: C ≻ D, D ≻ E. Forward loop: adds A ≻ C 0.80.
  4. Pass 3 Reverse loop: no remaining edge closes a cycle. Forward loop: skips A ≻ D 0.76 (already implied); adds A ≻ B 0.70.

Confidences are illustrative inputs; the graph computation is the paper’s Algorithm 1 (Section 3.3), run in your browser. Only heuristic edges become DPO pairs, so kept edges that lie on no cycle, such as the tree edge A ≻ E, are not trained on, and a fully consistent graph contributes no pairs. The resolved order is the kept graph with contradictory edges reversed (Property 2). Every confidence stays above the paper’s filter δ = 0.51; equal confidences are ordered by list position, which the paper does not specify. No model is queried or trained.

03 / Inside the method

Train on the evidence surrounding a contradiction

The algorithm first constructs a maximum spanning tree, preserving a connected set of strong comparisons. A reverse pass examines remaining edges from lower to higher confidence. When an edge closes a directed cycle, it is marked contradictory, while the existing edges along that cycle become candidate training evidence. A forward pass then considers stronger remaining edges, adding a new ordering relationship and skipping relationships already implied by a path.

An important detail is the final DPO dataset: it contains the supporting, or heuristic, edges selected around contradictions. The algorithm does not simply flip every suspicious label and train on the rewritten graph. Its intended effect is that learning the more reliable supporting comparisons will also change weaker inconsistent judgments.

The demo runs Algorithm 1 on five responses and ten illustrative judgments. Raising one confidence can move a wrong judgment into the kept structure, so that a correct comparison is flagged as contradictory and the wrong one becomes a DPO pair. This makes the assumption visible: higher confidence is treated as stronger evidence, so the procedure can produce a consistent ordering that is still factually wrong.

  1. 01

    Collect model preferences

    Sample responses and construct a directed graph from the model's pairwise judgments.

  2. 02

    Identify conflicting cycles

    Start with a maximum spanning tree and use confidence scores to locate contradictory edges.

  3. 03

    Train on reliable comparisons

    Select supporting preference pairs for DPO, encouraging the model to resolve weaker contradictions.

04 / Reading the evidence

Consistency improves, but it is not fully solved

  • 90.00%

    AdvBench safe-response rate

    Llama-2-7b-chat improves from 65.77% before alignment and 85.96% with confidence-only selection under the paper's automatic metric.

  • 4 tasks

    Alignment evaluation

    Experiments cover harm-free generation, instruction following, sentiment control, and summarization; preference-graph analysis also finds fewer contradictions.

The data-selection baselines use the same number of preference pairs, making their comparison informative about which pairs are chosen. On positive-sentiment generation, Llama-2-7b-chat reaches 87.2%, compared with 80.3% for maximum-confidence selection and 79.5% for random selection. The safety analysis also includes human assessment on 100 sampled AdvBench prompts; its reported harmless rate is 91% for ContraSolver and 86% for confidence-only selection.

Graph analysis provides a different outcome from task accuracy. For Llama-2-7b-chat on SafeEdit, the share of training inputs with a contradictory preference graph decreases from 13.3% to 10.4%. Contradictions therefore remain after model training, even though the graph-processing algorithm has a consistency property. These measurements use the original response nodes on training prompts, so they do not establish contradiction-free behavior on arbitrary new responses. Ties and confidence calibration remain limitations.

Research summary

While substantial advancements have been made in developing large language models (LLMs), achieving control over their behavior can be difficult. Direct preference optimization (DPO) assumes the existence of a latent reward function to evaluate the responses of LLMs. This assumption indicates a strict preference ordering of different responses to the same input. However, there always exist contradictions of preference in LLMs according to our experimental observations. In this paper, we construct a graph structure of the preference relationship among different responses with self-annotation to find contradictions in the preference order. We propose ContraSolver, an algorithm that traverses all edges on the preference graph to identify those that might cause contradictions. ContraSolver initializes the graph with a maximum spanning tree and identifies contradictory edges, prioritizing the resolution of low-confidence preferences while preserving high-confidence ones. Experimental results on four different generation tasks show that the performance of different LLMs can be largely improved through our completely unsupervised self-alignment. Furthermore, by analyzing the preference graphs of LLMs with and without self-alignment by ContraSolver, we quantify the reduction in contradictions, suggesting that resolving preference contradictions is crucial for achieving better alignment performance.
